title: AWS X-Ray tracing (segments, subsegments, and service map)
hook: AWS X-Ray traces requests across services as a tree of segments and subsegments. When CloudWatch shows high Lambda duration but logs look fine, the service map reveals which downstream call consumed the time.

blocks.text: A trace has a trace ID and segments per service. Subsegments cover internal work — HTTP calls, DynamoDB, SQL. Lambda active tracing creates segments automatically. SDK instrumentation adds subsegments. Sampling reduces cost — default 1 req/sec + 5% thereafter. Service map visualizes dependencies and error rates.

blocks.text: Logs tell you Lambda failed; X-Ray shows RDS query took 7 seconds. Missing propagation breaks trace at service boundaries. VPC cold start visible in init subsegment — proves ENI not business logic caused latency.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: enable active tracing on Lambda. Log trace_id in structured logs. Subsegments for external calls. Tune sampling for cost.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — Lambda active tracing
snippet.code:
Resources:
  PaymentProcessor:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: payment-processor
      TracingConfig:
        Mode: Active
      Runtime: nodejs20.x
      Handler: index.handler
snippet.explanation: Active mode creates X-Ray segment per invocation. PassThrough mode requires manual SDK setup.

snippet.explanation: trace_id in logs links Insights query to X-Ray console trace view.

snippet.explanation: Custom subsegments isolate business logic timing in trace waterfall.

snippet.label: CLI — get trace summaries by filter
snippet.code:
aws xray get-trace-summaries \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-1H +%s) \
  --end-time $(date -u +%s) \
  --filter-expression 'service(id(name: "payment-processor", type: "AWS::Lambda::Function")) { fault = true }'
snippet.explanation: Find fault traces for specific Lambda in last hour — faster than console browsing.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: No trace propagation across async SQS — broken trace. 100% sampling on high traffic — cost. Forgetting to instrument HTTP client — gap in waterfall. Confusing @requestId with trace ID.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: compare trace end-to-end duration to Lambda Duration metric — gap means missing subsegments. Init subsegment > 1s on VPC = ENI cold start evidence. Sampling rule: reservoir 1/sec + 5% + 100% on fault flag. X-Ray now integrates with CloudWatch Application Signals.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'X-Ray replaces logs.' Strong answer: traces show where time went; logs show why it failed; correlate with trace_id.

interviewTakeaways: Traces = segments per service + subsegments for downstream calls.
Lambda active tracing + captured AWS SDK clients for complete waterfall.
Log trace_id in structured logs to jump from Insights to X-Ray.
60s: Service map shows slow node. Init subsegment equals cold start. Sample to control cost. trace_id in logs.
Follow-up: how propagate trace across SQS async boundary?
commonPitfalls: Broken trace at SQS — no trace header in message attributes.
Strong answer: pass trace ID in message attribute; continue segment in consumer.
100% sampling on million RPS — cost rejection.
Uninstrumented fetch() call — mystery gap in trace.

jsTsCorrelations.note: OTel context propagation with traceparent header is W3C standard — X-Ray uses X-Amzn-Trace-Id; ADOT bridges both.
Flame chart in DevTools parallels X-Ray waterfall — nested timing blocks for nested async calls.
